feasible

/FEE-zuh-bul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Feasible means capable of being done or carried out; practically possible.

Finishing the treehouse in one weekend was feasible only because the lumber had already been cut to size.

Example

The student council wanted to host a spring carnival. Before approving it, the principal asked one question: was the plan feasible? The treasurer priced the tents and games against the club's savings, the custodian confirmed the field would be free that weekend, and enough volunteers signed up to cover every booth. With the budget, the space, and the workers all accounted for, the council showed the carnival could realistically be carried out.

The council proved the carnival could actually be done with the money, space, and volunteers available, which is exactly what feasible means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

achievable: Achievable means able to be accomplished, and it points at the goal — a target, a score, a deadline. Feasible points at the plan for getting there: can this project realistically be carried out with the time, money, and resources at hand? A goal is achievable; the schedule for reaching it is feasible or it is not.

workable: Workable describes a design or arrangement good enough to function once tried — a workable compromise, a workable seating chart. Feasible asks the prior question: whether the plan can realistically be carried out at all with the time, money, and resources available. A layout can be workable on paper while the renovation it requires is not feasible this year.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

impossible: not able to be done at all

futile: pointless because it cannot succeed

Where it sits · how easily it can really be done

possible → feasible → effortless

possible vs. feasible: A possible plan could happen in theory, while a feasible one can realistically be carried out with the time, money, and resources at hand.

effortless vs. feasible: A feasible project can be done with real effort and planning, but an effortless one practically completes itself.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — feas: from Latin facere, to do or make, by way of Old French faisable, doable

Suffix — -ible: able to be

Put it together: Feasible entered English from Old French faisable, 'doable,' built ultimately on Latin facere, 'to do or make,' the same root behind factory and manufacture. A feasible plan is, quite literally, one that can be done.

Use the root in a new word: facilitate: A good checklist can facilitate even a complicated move; hers ran to three pages and saved the day twice.

Word Choice

neutral; planning, business, and engineering register

Feasible describes plans, projects, budgets, and timelines, things to be carried out, and asks whether they can realistically be done with the time, money, and resources available. Related but distinct: plausible judges whether a claim or explanation seems believable, while feasible judges whether a plan can actually be executed; a plausible business idea may still not be feasible on a student budget.
